paragraphs.source_en: The night of the twenty-sixth day of the eighth month in the first year of Tenshō. Standing before his field headquarters on Mount Toragozen, Oda Nobunaga gazed at the scattered lights of Odani Castle, where Azai Nagamasa and his father dwelt, and sank deep into thought. The moon had not yet risen; stars glittered across the sky, and now and then the neighing of warhorses sounded from the darkness. Beside Nobunaga stood Kinoshita Hideyoshi, who had already taken the surname Hashiba, and Niwa Gorōzaemon; for some reason, both remained silent.

But Hisamasa and his son were different. paragraphs.source_en: Hideyoshi understood both the breadth of Nobunaga’s vision and the anxiety within him. Honganji Kōsa, who was related by marriage to the Asakura house of Echizen, was seeking aid from the monks of Kii in hopes of inciting an uprising before Odani Castle fell. At Namazue Castle in Ōmi, Rokkaku Yoshisuke was also stirring restlessly. If Nobunaga allowed private feelings to make him miss the moment for battle, the daimyō of Chūgoku and Shikoku, as well as the forces of northern Ise, would seize their chance to move. Nobunaga therefore meant to concentrate an army powerful enough to overwhelm the enemy around Mount Toragozen and force the Azai father and son to submit.
